Accountability · Post Office · Opinion

Kemi blamed the government machine. She was one of its ministers.

Post Office compensation delays, ministerial responsibility and the limits of blaming bureaucracy.

Steve English · Originally published 15 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch’s account of the Post Office compensation delays raises a straightforward question about leadership.

If you recognise that a system is failing people, hold ministerial responsibility and still cannot get it moving quickly enough, how much credit should you receive for recognising the problem?

Giving evidence to the Horizon inquiry in November 2024, Badenoch described frustration with bureaucracy, Treasury requirements and the slow delivery of compensation.

She said she had asked why victims could not simply be given their money. When questioned about who had allowed bureaucracy to obstruct redress, she identified “the Government machine”.

She also acknowledged that the ITV drama had helped move matters forward.

That explanation deserves examination from someone now asking voters to trust her to run the country.

THE ROW THAT DOMINATED THE HEADLINES

Earlier that year, Badenoch had become embroiled in a public confrontation with Henry Staunton, whom she dismissed as Post Office chairman in January 2024.

Staunton alleged that a senior official had conveyed that compensation spending should be slowed before the election.

Badenoch vigorously rejected his account. In Parliament, she accused him of spreading falsehoods and defended his dismissal on governance and conduct grounds.

The later inquiry findings matter: Sir Wyn Williams rejected Staunton’s interpretation of his conversation with permanent secretary Sarah Munby. He concluded that she had said nothing which could reasonably be understood as suggesting compensation should be stalled.

That particular accusation cannot fairly be presented as a proven Conservative plot.

But rejecting it does not erase the failures in delivering redress.

SHE DID PUSH FOR FASTER PAYMENTS

The inquiry examined Badenoch’s August 2023 letter to Jeremy Hunt seeking measures to accelerate compensation.

She supported a proposed £100,000 fixed payment for claimants in the Group Litigation Order scheme and described her willingness to challenge value-for-money objections.

There is evidence that she wanted faster action. Any honest assessment must recognise it.

However, counsel also asked why she had not assumed that level of engagement earlier. Badenoch said she would not initially have known enough and described the letter as following months of frustration.

That leaves a legitimate political question: was her intervention sufficiently early, sustained and effective?

WHY DID TELEVISION CHANGE THE CALCULATION?

Badenoch’s explanation of the ITV drama’s impact was revealing.

She told the inquiry that it shifted the issue from value for money towards public perception, and that it made things happen.

The victims’ suffering had existed before television brought it into millions of living rooms.

A government should be capable of responding decisively to documented injustice before public pressure makes delay politically unbearable.

Badenoch’s evidence describes a minister struggling to overcome her own government’s machinery. Voters are entitled to ask what that says about her effectiveness—and about the Conservative government’s priorities.

THE RECORD IS BIGGER THAN THE PERSONAL FEUD

In July 2025, Sir Wyn’s report found that Horizon Shortfall Scheme claimants had not received full and fair redress. He criticised unnecessarily adversarial approaches to substantial claims and called for urgent reforms.

Those findings concern institutions and decisions spanning different administrations. They are not a finding that Badenoch personally caused every delay.

They nevertheless expose the distance between repeated government assurances and victims’ experiences.

Badenoch can point to letters, proposals and her frustration with officials. Those are relevant parts of her record.

So are the delays.

Leadership must ultimately be judged by what changes for the people waiting—not simply by how strongly a minister says she wanted change.
